utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, and I'm here with Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin. And I got distracted because our transcript doesn't seem to be working over here on this. I was going to go over and fix it, and then I thought I heard you say "appearances for Mr. Brdjanin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a moment I thought you were checking -- we were. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you too. Anything before we start. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first relates to the witness. I received a message this morning from VWS that Mr. Filipovic, who Your Honours I'm not sure are probably aware of yet, because he hasn't covered it, had to have part of his foot amputated as a result of the treatment. He complained that his foot was causing him some pain, and he was taken to the doctor at around midday. He's back. He says -- and can I say straight away, by chance I ran into him with the VWS person as he was being taken to the witness waiting room, so I took the opportunity -- I didn't imagine anybody would object -- to ask him -- and the VWS person was there -- just about his health. He says he's prepared to go on this afternoon. His foot is still causing him discomfort. I'm not sure if he was given medication. I think he needs something to rest his foot on. And I said to him that if he felt tired in any way, that he should immediately inform Your Honours, and no doubt Your Honours will have the same observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Ms. Korner, for that and also for the part -- for the interest you took. And actually, I did yesterday -- I did notice at some point that he was getting tired and fed up. I did ask him actually whether he was tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there was a moment when we approached 5.00 he was appearing tired and also fed up. And when he stood up to -- for one of the breaks, he could hardly walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I found he had difficulty in getting started, let's put it like that. I will tell him myself. But in any case, I mean, you know by now that this is something that I take seriously and we will do whatever is necessary. In the meantime, I don't know -- there is in Courtroom III, if there is no one sitting there -- there is a footrest which is not mine. I mean, I'm intruding where -- where I shouldn't. But in Courtroom III there is a footrest which perhaps if the Presiding Judge is not using, we could -- we could borrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But that's not high enough. The one there is -- in room 3 -- Courtroom III is much better, because it can be moved and placed high or low as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps while I deal with the other matters, that perhaps the -- one of the court staff could make inquiries as to whether there is such a footrest available. Your Honour, the second matter is the investigator Mr. Dupas and an interpreter went over to the hotel this morning to speak to another witness. They were spotted by Mr. Filipovic, who apparently overnight made some inquiries in Banja Luka or -- not in Banja Luka, I imagine, but somewhere about the name of this reporter and has come up with the name of Zimmerman, we think. So I'm passing that on for consideration. Mr. Zecevic just for Your Honours, said that although there's a reference to TV Banja Luka at the end of this particular documentary, it doesn't specifically say it's a production of TV Banja Luka, and I accept that of course. I think it -- Mr. Zecevic can probably help more about that. But as I say, that's the latest information we've got. I don't know whether Mr. Zecevic wants to tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I just informed Ms. Korner that I watched the tape again last night, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're lucky. You've seen it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw it probably five times by now. I know it by heart. The point is that at the very end of the part which Ms. Korner would like to show before -- before the -- this Trial Chamber and in this courtroom is the -- is an advertisement of -- asking the people who do not have registered TV appliances to register them with the TV Banja Luka at a certain address in Banja Luka. That is the only reference which refers to TV Banja Luka. So it might be assumed by that that it -- this particular piece has been aired on TV Banja Luka, but it -- at no point does it say that it's a production of TV Banja Luka or any other production for that matter. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And does the name Zimmerman ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would be very -- I would be very surprised that there is a journalist in Banja Luka by the name of Zimmerman. I haven't heard so far anybody -- a journalist by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My co-counsel is saying there was an American ambassador in Belgrade before the war Zimmerman, but I don't think that's the same person. So I -- we are not aware of any journalist by the surname Zimmerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second matter relates to the witness who should have been the next witness whom I've applied for protective measures. I say "should have been." Your Honour, it's become abundantly clear that we can't call him and therefore we're not going to call him. The next witness, therefore, will be Witness 7.196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And -- who hasn't got any --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Protective measures, no. Your Honour, I'm being careful because basically you never know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I am careful there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The proposed order thereafter for next week, depending on whether 7.196 is able to start on Monday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he a crime-based witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, and no. In other words, he has a certain amount of information about the resistance. So if -- yes, he's a crime-based witness in the sense he's going to give evidence about a particular incident, but he's also able to deal with those matters. And I'm anticipating that he's likely to be some time in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thereafter, Witness 7.135, 7. -- as it is, they're all being lined up for next week. Your Honour, we are replacing the witness that we can't call with another witness from the same area, and his statement has been disclosed to the Defence today, and he'll come at the end of the -- the Kljuc municipality. And we still have one gentleman left from Sanski Most who we're going to be calling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and then finally that just brings me very briefly on to the question of timing and Prijedor. At the rough -- best rough guess, we would finish Kljuc municipality at -- on or about the 20th of September -- the 19th, we estimate it, which is a Thursday. And therefore would probably start Prijedor on the 23rd of September. I, as I said earlier or said yesterday, I agree with Mr. Ackerman that it may be productive for there to be a meeting between the Prosecution and Defence before we start the municipality. The week of the 30th is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And therefore, it may be sufficient for one day plus the weekend and to start on the 23rd. But certainly we'll know closer to the time, and I think certainly at least one day off to discuss how to deal with it. The tapes of the previous testimony of witnesses in the Stakic case we're told should be available by Monday, the B/C/S tapes. I'm not sure that I know about the other testimony. All right. Well, that -- they'll be supplied to us by Monday, but apparently of course they have to be edited so that closed session -- all the stuff comes out. But I -- well, Your Honour, I can deal with that. But can I just mention one things: I was contacted by the registrar today about sitting dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether we could swap. Your Honour, I understand there won't be -- Bosanski Samac, the Simic case is finished. So I understand there may be a courtroom available for an all-day sitting, in the sense of not all-day in the hours we've been sitting morning and afternoon, but if we were to do the type of Milosevic hours, 9.30 through till 1.00 and then whatever. I don't know whether Your Honours have considered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have considered it. But before we tell you what our preference is, I would like to know what Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Zecevic think about it. In other words, the options that seem to be open are to either switch to morning sessions, starting at 9.00 and finishing at quarter to 2.00. Alternatively, have the old regime schedule in place, starting at 9.30, finishing at quarter to 1.00, I think, or something like that, and then start again at 2.00, I think, or something like that and finish at 4.00. I know that your preference, Ms. Korner, is to have this -- the full day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is, for two -- can I explain. For two reasons: One is you don't have quite the sort of compression and the need to move. And it gives us extra sitting time, and it would be nice to finish Prijedor by the beginning of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I doubt. What's the total daily hours, Chuqing, in the old system, say, in the Milosevic trial, when they start at 9.00 and finish at 1.00, how many hours do they sit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's four hours, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four hours, 30 minutes. And we sit --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Three hours, 45 minutes currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there's a three-quarter of an hour difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's quite a major difference, Your Honours if you add it up over the week. And the other thing, as Your Honour knows -- and I know it's an OTP problem, which might be avoided. But Stakic is during one part of it, although I'm going to attempt to persuade Judge Schomburg -- hopefully I'm going to persuade Judge Schomburg to say that these deliberations shouldn't take place, but there will be the -- the submissions under Rule 98 and the oral arguments at some stage. I think the first week in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he told me. I mean -- but I didn't jot down the dates at the time, because I didn't think it was important for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's -- may I say the deliberations are a concept that escape me entirely at the moment, so I'm appearing before him, I hope, tomorrow morning to ask him about this. But as I understand, he set aside a week at the beginning of October to hear oral argument on Rule 98 submissions. Now, I agree, I can't see how it can take a week, because written motions will be put in by both sides. But that would cause the problem. And the other problem would be once we start Prijedor, in order to minimise the necessity for witnesses to come up early to see different lawyers, the same lawyers that called the witnesses in the Stakic case will be used to call the witnesses in this case. So that's why I -- as I say, that is the preference we have for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the -- yes. Can anyone enlighten me on the position regarding the 28th October to November 1, November 1st? That doesn't seem -- would -- Simic would have restarted by then, no?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will restart on the 21st of October in the Simic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So the last week of -- let's start from last week of October. It cannot be changed in any case. What I'm trying to do is to fill in where there is a court maintenance day off. If we could switch chamber -- courtroom -- if we could switch courtroom, we could add one day, and that can make us recover all these 30 minutes or 45 minutes difference that there may be between one system and another. What are your options, anyway? Let's start with Mr. Ackerman. I always start with Mr. Ackerman not out of disrespect, Mr. Zecevic. Just because it's just more convenient. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, our preference is -- my preference is that we work the morning schedule as much we can, because I prefer mornings to afternoons, for a lot of reasons. The largest problem that I face in this case is not being able to find sufficient preparation time, and it's extraordinarily difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That I share with you, because I -- I speak for myself, but I also know that my colleagues have the same problem. When you finish here at 6.30 -- and we finish at 6.30, not 7.00. Apart from the amount of energy that is left in you and -- I mean, one has to -- I mean, I have to look after myself, and that leaves me with very little time for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the morning when I come here, even though I have an afternoon sitting, I'm still dealing with 101 things that come up, be it Nikolic, Mrksic, Merdja, Blagojevic, and et cetera and I end up having to read documents or agree to decisions or disagree to decisions. So basically you end up coming here at 8.00 in the morning and returning home at 7.00 at night and that's 11 hours, leaving you very little time for anything else. So my preference definitely would be for morning sessions too. What about Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we absolutely agree. It is our preference as well. And we have the same problem. As you know, even more, because I came into the case rather late. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But by now -- by now you give me the impression you have recovered the lost --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I did my best. But anyhow, we are now faced with the Prijedor case -- the part of the case which is actually pertaining to the municipality of Prijedor. Most of the witnesses which are -- which are going to be called over here have already been testified, some of them even four times. What we are getting from the OTP is thousands of pages of transcript of material of the witness's testimony over here in other cases. I mean, we really do need a lot of time to prepare for each and every witness because we cannot really afford to just forget about his previous testimonies or whatever. So in that case -- and most of all, because of that, we would prefer the morning schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- you know, I can see when I'm outvoted. I mean, the only reason I was asked when this case was going to end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I understand, Ms. Korner. I understand the interest that you have to get this over and done with. What I would like to ask you to check -- not you personally obviously. Get someone from your staff or have the Registry do this exercise -- whether we can steal a day, because I notice that the week of the 9th September to 13th September, that's -- we are already morning sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's when there was a court maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next week Friday. Friday, the 13th is court maintenance. So if we could find a courtroom available -- Courtroom III is court maintenance. Courtroom II -- Courtroom II in the afternoon -- Courtroom II in the afternoon, as far as I read my schedule, my agenda, Stakic seems to be sitting from 9.00 to 13.45 but not in the afternoon. So if we could utilise with obviously the concurrence of the Defence as well -- if we could steal that afternoon and have an extra sitting on that day, on Friday, the 13th in Courtroom II, we would at least gain -- gain something like three and a half hours. That would be at least one thing that I can recommend to you. Otherwise -- otherwise it seems we have 16th September to 20th September when we can move to the morning. And that would be where Simic is sitting, Courtroom III. And in that week I notice, Madam Chuqing, that at least in my -- again, that Galic seems to have also a sitting on the 20th of September in Courtroom III, although it is in italics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm anxious obviously to get Mr. Filipovic going. I wonder if we could perhaps try and come to -- to some sort of arrangement. I mean, it -- I heard Judge Schomburg this morning announcing how much it costs to run court each day, but one of the reasons really is that -- and I've raised it before and I don't know whether administration -- I cannot understand why we should be forced to lose a whole day for court maintenance on -- you know, every three weeks. I really can't. And it does seem to me that this constant, constant days off because of court maintenance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we seem to get them all in this case. We seem to get them all. Actually, we have got special treatment in the sense that we -- now it's changing, but we had one-third morning sittings, two-thirds afternoon sittings, which I didn't like and which I contested. But then also the rest seems -- we switch courtrooms only to find that we switch in the week when there is a courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- court maintenance, and it ends up some months we have two or three courtroom maintenance days off. It's unfortunate, because I would rather sit a whole -- a whole week than have a Friday off just because there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think perhaps one ought to make it clear to the administration in this building that outside of Milosevic, this is possibly the biggest case running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's certainly the -- the most document-heavy, and it's one that ought to get treatment that doesn't mean unnecessary unless asked for by Defence or UN holidays, unnecessary days all. I mean, literally somebody in the team counted up the sitting days in October, and it's something like 13 because of court maintenance and whatever. And 13 out of a potential, what is it, four weeks -- 20 days-odd sitting is ridiculous, absolutely ridiculous. And if you know -- the general public are going to worry about the length of time these trials take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. In October -- in October we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But by the way, let's not lose -- waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyway, Your Honour, I've made the point. I keep on making it. But we keep on being told that general public won't stand for these long trials. What they don't understand is that these trials do not sit anything like proper court days or five days a week. And anyhow, I've made that point before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, please liaise with the Registry to see what changes we need to make after you have consulted also with Judge Schomburg tomorrow with regard to the dates when Stakic is sitting so that we try to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's just the only potential conflict on Prijedor, Your Honour, would come on that first week in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Other than that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will find me behind you if you need -- whatever you need there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in order to avoid any -- any unnecessary waste of time or clashes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So let's -- usher, the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Filipovic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Welcome back. I kindly ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, before you continue giving evidence, I understand that you had some health problems today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to see a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any problem throughout your stay in this courtroom, if you need to rest, if you need a break -- a short break, if you're tired, if you want to stop, you only have to say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not here to make your life difficult. We appreciate the fact that you have come here to give evidence. And certainly we do not wish to put you in a position where you have to be inconvenienced more than by the fact of giving evidence. So let me know -- just make me a sign, stop me, and say "I'm not feeling well. I'm tired. I would like to stop here or I would like a break, or whatever, and you will be given all the attention that you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner. Examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I was going to come on to the events of the 26th of May onwards, but you mentioned yesterday and we looked at some documents relating to dismissal of non-Serb personnel. And I just want to deal with that as a general topic before dealing with the major events. Could you be handed, please, Exhibit 973.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which I think that Your Honours will find in volume 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Volume 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Volume 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Filipovic, this is the -- a document from -- it looks like the Sanica wood processing plant, addressed to the Kljuc Municipal Assembly and dated the 21st of June, "Re information on managerial staff with reference to your correspondence, the 18th of June, we hereby forward you information regarding the situation in the managerial staff of Muslim and Croatian nationality who perform the duties at the level of foreman and above." Just looking at that list of names, did you know any of those people personally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without mentioning -- going through each name, how many of them roughly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 12 and 13 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did they all lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now have P974. Again, this is on the same topic. The date of this document is two days later, the 23rd of June, and relates to a wood processing plant and other enterprises. Did you know people who are named there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those whom you knew, did they lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. One of them during the war worked as a cleaning man, but he was otherwise an engineer. And as he remained in Kljuc throughout the war, he cleaned the streets as a member of the public utility company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which one was that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 1 from joint services, Eniz Pobric. He was also a member of the business board and one of the managerial staff members of this company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now look, please, at 978. This starts -- again, this is a list of various companies and enterprises which starts with the municipal assembly. And did -- leaving aside the municipal assembly because the Muslims left, but people who had jobs there, are you able to say just looking at that first page, did those people that you knew lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. From the 27th of May onwards, not one of them was working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then could you look now, please, at 983.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that this document is the subject of dispute, or objected to -- documents, I should say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision relieving Mr. Kapetanovic of his duty as a judge; pointing -- the next document, a Mr. Dmitrovic. These documents are dated in July. And then the next document, your brother is relieved of his duties as vice-president of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. On the 21st of July, where was your brother, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the Manjaca concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we can see that there are various decisions relieving people of their jobs, all those mentioned to do with the municipal assembly and judges. Who was -- there's a lady mentioned called Merima Filipovic, secretary of the municipal secretariat. Was she a relation of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my sister-in-law, the wife of my late brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes. And if we -- still on the same topic, could you be handed 1017, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That is in volume ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's volume 2 as well, Your Honour. These are all in volume 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's behind divider 51 in mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just turn over the page. Is that the signature of Mr. Banjac? If you could turn over the page and have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It says: "On the 7th of August, 1992 the War Presidency, as it was then called, stated that all state organs and socially owned mixed and public enterprises and public institutions in Kljuc shall dismiss the following workers: All workers who participated in the armed uprising and are currently in prison in Manjaca, near Banja Luka, or on the run; all workers who did not respond to military mobilisation; all workers who did not respond to work obligation. And the public security station and Kljuc municipal secretariat for National Defence shall submit details of these individuals at the request of organs, companies, and communities." Again, in reality, who were the people who were in Manjaca or did not respond to military mobilisation or did not respond to work obligation? What nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats. For example, my wife got a call-up paper for mobilisation. She refused, and she was dismissed from her job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that away. And then the final group. If you go, please -- if you could be handed 1023 and 1024, please. This covers 5, 6, 7. This is Kljuc court. It is the remit of the commission to implement disciplinary proceedings against employees who have been absent from work without explanation during June, July, and August. And on the basis of established state of facts to adopt a suitable decision or ruling, there are a number of these rulings. And if we look at P0 -- P1024, we see that disciplinary proceedings were taken against an employee named Fedhija Eljezovic, resident of Kljuc assigned to the position of an enforcement clerk in the court for having missed more than three consecutive days of work in the period from 28 May to 3 June. By any chance did you know this person, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a lady, Ms. Fedhija Eljezovic, and I did know her personally. She was the secretary of the president of the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it said that she didn't turn up for work on the 28th of May to the 3rd of June. And do you know why she didn't turn up for work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one has to laugh at that question. She couldn't come. The whole of Kljuc at that time was buzzing with policemen and soldiers. And if a person of Muslim or Croatian ethnicity came out, immediately - and I apologise for using a Bosnian word - it would be addressed with the words "Where are you, balija? Fuck balijas. Kill the Ustashas." So no one dared come out of their houses for the whole period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Filipovic. That's all I'm going to ask you about dismissals, except maybe just one last -- I'm sorry, one last document. 1034, please. This is a letter apparently from the forestry enterprise that we saw addressed to the -- dated the 4th of September, 1992, addressed to the municipal assembly, the War Presidency. "Since in certain enterprises and institutions at the level of Kljuc municipality the employees of Croatian and Muslim nationality are treated differently, in the sense of continuing to carry out their duties and assignments, as well as the calculation of salaries, we would like you to tell us what to do in that regard when employees of our enterprise are in question." Actually, and I don't need to ask you anything about that. Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. Yes, thank you. If you could give that back to the usher. Now, Mr. Filipovic, I want to ask you about the events of the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. But we started the day with Ms. Korner complaining that we don't have time to get through these things, and then she's reading documents without asking questions, which is just taking up time unnecessarily it seems to me. She just went through this document, read it to us, and said she had no question about it. And she's been doing that. She's doing what I complain about her wanting to read documents. So when she gets a witness here, she reads the documents in the guise of asking questions, but then she doesn't ask questions. She just reads the document. If we really want to move rapidly through this, I think we can dispense of the document reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've been over this over and over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't reply and we proceed, we can get there quicker.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just making the point, this case, as I said earlier, is about documents. And somehow these documents have got to be made part of the court record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Could you be handed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We are getting to the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's now the 27th of May. And I'm going to use for the basis the report that was written about that, Your Honour. That's Exhibit 1012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In which --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's in bundle -- binder 2 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 1012.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if the witness could be handed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Filipovic, this is a report that was written in July of 1992 apparently by the Banja Luka services centre or by the Kljuc SJB on the events that happened in Kljuc. And I think you've had an opportunity to read through it before. It -- there's a general background to begin with. And if we just look at the beginning, the introductory notes, it goes through the inhabitants of Kljuc and states, as we've looked at before, that there was a decrease in the members of Serbs who lived there. And you've already explained to us about that. It then goes through the events -- the attitude towards the Yugoslav crisis, the attitude to mobilisation, the status of the municipality in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And perhaps we should just look at one of the things that's said there, under paragraph 4, where it talks about the decision to join Kljuc to the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, a decision in which May of 1991, a decision which was confirmed in December of 1991. And then it goes on to state that "Since it was clear that the idea of a unitary BH was not going to win the day, all the activities of the SDA and the Muslim Bosniak organisation were directed towards the dividing of the municipality and the creating of a Muslim municipality. From the security aspect, the distribution of the population in the municipality was exceptionally unpropitious since more than 70 per cent of Muslims lived in the north-west part of the municipality, which borders on Sanski Most." Then it deals with the work of Kljuc, the SJB. And it then goes on to deal with what it calls the goals of the armed rebellion. And it states this: "Two whole months have passed since the Muslim extremists and fundamentalists started an armed rebellion in the area of Kljuc municipality. Their activities were coordinated over the entire area of the Bosnian Krajina and the centre of the armed rebellion was located in the area of the Prijedor-Kozarac municipality with the intention of spreading it in all directions." Leaving out the rest of this description, "The main goals of the rebellion were the destruction of the legally elected organs of government; 2, the weakening of the fighting power of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH; 3, the withdrawal of our units from the front line and the creation of room for manoeuvre for the forces of the Republic of Croatia." Now, Mr. Filipovic, do you agree with this assertion that there was an armed rebellion which had those goals, an armed rebellion by the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. That is not true. Because there's this paragraph on page 8 where it says that "All our information points to the fact that the Muslim Territorial Defence was formed primarily for defensive action."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to come to that. Let's just deal, then, with what's put under "Operational information." "Previous operational work had established that in addition to the regular forces of the Serbian Republic of BH, there was a parallel system of Muslim Territorial Defence in existence on the territory of the Kljuc municipality. The officially appointed commander was a reserve sergeant, Omer Filipovic," and gives his positions. "And it was known that the internal organisation of the Muslim Territorial Defence was similar to our own organisational scheme." And it goes on to suggest that, as the Muslims had not responded to mobilisation, the majority of reserve officers formed detachments, platoons, and companies on the principle of functional organisation in local communities." And then it talks about the Green Berets. And then it says this: "All this information pointed with great certainty to the fact that the Muslim Territorial Defence was primarily being organised to perform defence activities. Their guards were protecting only the approaches to villages, while a system of defence was established on the edge and within each village." Do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I insist that we were preparing exclusively for defence and not for any attack, and I persist in denying what it says in the report of the public security station, that is, that the illegal commander was, they were legal. I claim that they were illegal and that we were legal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It then talks about in the next paragraph that the orders of officers were executed unquestioningly. The Muslim clergy also played an active part in everything." As far as you were concerned, what was the role played by the Muslim clergy, as so described?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim clergy played an exclusively religious role. And on Fridays, at the prayers, if there was any talk, then they would say, "Let's get ready for what lies in wait," quite opposite to what Serbian religious officials were doing, who were instigating ethnic unrest. So I claim with responsibility that the Muslim and Croat religious officials in Kljuc tried to bring back to reason the people and exclusively during the time of prayers, because it was not allowed to hold any such meetings in mosques and Catholic churches outside of those times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on then to the next paragraph: "Later operational work established they did not find organising either easy or simple. Their main reasons for this were their fears that in conflict with the Serbs, they could only be defeated. Their belief that they did not have any reason or motive to attack their neighbours and their trust in the official organs of authority in the municipality. An additional problem for the majority of Muslims was securing the financial means to purchase weapons, since these weapons could only be bought for foreign currency." Would you agree that that was a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. In those days in Kljuc you couldn't buy anything for Yugoslav dinars because there was the machinery operating in Belgrade Topcider and they printed so many dinars and sent them to Bosnian Krajina that there were dealers who had boots full of dinars buying foreign currency from the people, the aim being to carry foreign exchange from Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, so that it was not possible to buy anything except with foreign currency or gold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it goes on in the next paragraph to say, or to assert that "By means of determined propaganda to the effect that they would be physically liquidated by the Serbs, the SDA and MBO leaderships together with the most extreme members of the younger generation of Muslims, every day gained more adherence as a result of their crazy indoctrination. Under the pretext of preparing for the defence of their villages and houses, the Muslims were developing a system of defence and organising their Territorial Defence. All our information points to the fact that the Muslim Territorial Defence was in fact formed primarily for defence activities." And let's stop there. You referred us to that line already, Mr. Filipovic. But the suggestion is that it was propaganda that you and the SDA were putting out to -- that you would be physically - you the Muslims - would be physically liquidated by Serbs. First of all, were you asserting, were you saying these things?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That proved to be true subsequently, that we were right. The subsequent course of events proved that we were right. In Kljuc between 800 and 1.000 men and civilians were killed. So whatever we had alleged were later confirmed by the events, and this showed that we had been right and that we had told our people the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the paragraph goes on to say that "Operational work carried out established that a number of meetings were held in Prijedor and Sanski Most in May." Pausing there. You've already dealt with those. "At which the decision to initiate an armed rebellion was made, and their intention was to achieve the goals enumerated above. "The change in concept switching from defensive to offensive activities had disastrous consequences for the Muslims living in the area of Kljuc municipality. The attacks that they mounted on the 27th of May, 1992 gave the army of the Serbian Republic of BH every right to take energetic action to settle accounts with the organisers and participants in these activities." And now let's come to the combat activities that, as they put it, that day. "Combat activities in the area of Kljuc municipality started on the 27th of May, 1992. On that day, Muslim extremists and fundamentalists carried out a number of synchronised combat actions against members of the police force and the army of Serbian BH which were intended to destroy the bulk of our forces on the front line and thus weaken our positions." And then they set out -- I'll come back to what they say about synchronised, but let's look at the account of the actions. They start with what they say is the setting of ambushes in the area of Gornji Ramici. And it is -- and I'm summarising this, it's alleged that roadblocks had been set up on the approach to the village, that a traffic patrol and military police went there, that they were fired upon, and that Mr. Stojakovic, the assistant commander of Kljuc, was killed and two other people injured -- in fact, three. And then it goes on to say: "Immediately thereafter, a representative of the public security station arrived at the scene of the incident and negotiated with commanders of the unit in the presence of Omer Filipovic. And he promised that a team of experts could go to the scene." Now, firstly, were you there when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. I was not. Only I'd like to make a correction here. Whoever wrote this report, this has nothing to do with Gornji Ramici. This was in the area of Krasulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But were you aware of an incident in which Mr. Stojakovic was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any involvement by your brother in the incident or its aftermath?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother did not participate. He was just there as security so that Vinko Kondic could come on site, because the inhabitants of the village of Krasulje would not let anyone pass without Omer. However, Omer's presence was a guarantee that Vinko and all the others who came would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear any accounts of that incident from anyone who was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards, but not on the 27th, because I was imprisoned on the 28th. But from Omer I heard by phone, because I'd remained in Kljuc, and Omer called me up and he told me that a problem had cropped up, and he explained what it was all about by phone. And following that event, I learnt of this when -- from people in Gradiska, in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look at what they describe as the second incident, an ambush in the area of Busija and the village of Pudin Han. This was a -- there was a convoy, and I think there's been mention of it before -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't notice that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. But the witness has said at 28, line 22. He said, "Because I remained in Kljuc -- and he says "I was supposed to remain in Kljuc." And it's -- it hasn't been translated. It might be fairly important in my opinion. If this can be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Filipovic, you've heard what Mr. Zecevic has just pointed out. In your testimony, did you just say that you had remained in Kljuc or that you were to remain in Kljuc, or expected --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remained there, and I was supposed to remain there, to be with the people, because the others went to Velagici and Krasulje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can we look at the second incident that's described, where the allegation was that there were unarmed soldiers travelling from Knin to Banja Luka which was a convoy ambushed. The ambush set on both sides of the road, some 80 extremists took part in it. And the operation was organised and commanded by Amir Avdic and Nedzad Djeric. What do you know about that incident, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found out about the incident when I was imprisoned on -- captured on the 28th, and then when I was beaten and then they said, "So you were the one who ordered that young Yugoslav soldiers should be killed." And this was the first time I heard about it, on the 28th at the police station. I didn't know about that. I hadn't known about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amir Avdic, was he imprisoned in Manjaca with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Amir Avdic, he made a breakthrough through Sjlaka [phoen]. He imprisoned -- captured some of the high-ranking Serb soldiers, officers, and then he was able to go to Bihac, and then he became one of the commanders of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you learnt about it, first of all, when you were beaten, and then when you were in Manjaca. Did you learn about it from someone who was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those who were from Velagici, if they were not directly in that part, because Velagici is a village --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm sorry. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this happened in an area of a few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not the Velagici incident. We've already heard evidence of that. The incident of Pudin Han, that's described here.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is all, Madam Prosecutor. This is all one thing. We residents, we made a distinction and we called it Pudin Han because the whole area in fact was Velagici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But was there somebody who had taken part in this so-called ambush who told you what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While I was in Stara Gradiska and Manjaca, I was ill. I couldn't move. You saw my pictures. I only -- I was only able to start walking when I came to London to be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then can we look, please, at the third incident that's described here, the setting of an ambush in Tocina. "On the same day, in the immediate vicinity of the junction in Pudin Han and in the area called Tocina, an ambush was set in which between 20 and 30 extremists took part. Operational work revealed that there had been some hesitation on the part of the some participants in the ambush who had refrained from attacking the police patrol." Do you know anything about that incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "4, the blowing up of the M-5 road between Velagici and Laniste." An attempt was made to carry out -- the blast was carried out with 80 kilos of explosive but did not have more significant effect. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that. But with 80 kilogrammes of explosive, you can blow -- you can bring down this building. But I don't know anything specific about this event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then an attack on a checkpoint in Velagici. In one -- in the attack a policeman, Mr. Marijanovic, was hit with three bullets in his bulletproof jacket. It doesn't say whether he was killed or not. And then finally, 6, the capture of seven soldiers of the Serbian Army of BH in the village of, one I can never pronounce, Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I think you started -- you started to tell us about that, Mr. Filipovic, and I think you do know something about this incident.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that it happened on the 25th. And as I told you yesterday, Atif Dedic came and informed Omer and myself about what had happened, and I know about -- that much about the incident, that people were captured but that Omer strictly stated that nothing should be done to them, that they would in future be used for exchange purposes. And I don't know any more about the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, it is said in that paragraph that began that these were "synchronised combat actions against members of the police force and the Army of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina intended to destroy the bulk of our forces on the front line." Now, was -- as far as you're concerned, as one of the members of the Muslim TO and Crisis Staff, were these synchronised attacks intended to destroy the Serbian police and army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. I keep insisting on the fact that we were defending ourselves, Crljeni specifically has no connection or no relation with other villages, so we were not equipped as well as the Serb army. The Serb army had radio transmitters, and we hadn't -- the people from Crljeni didn't have any contact with Muslim people from the surrounding villages. So we cannot speak of synchronised action at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then it says this, in paragraph 7, "Deployment of our forces." And that may be where we have to break. "On the same day, the command of the 30th Division issued an order to deploy units of the Army of the Serbian Republic. On the next day negotiations commenced to retrieve bodies of the dead, the injured person with the surname of Despot and to save the seven captured soldiers. All these activities were carried out successfully and without any casualties among our forces. The operation of the 30th Division reinforced by forces of the Kljuc public security station was carried out rapidly, energetically, and efficiently. The resistance of the extremists and fundamentalists was crushed. On that occasion, our forces inflicted serious casualties on them and a certain quantity of their weapons used in the armed resistance was destroyed. In the next few days, the military policeman Milorad Markovic died in combat while performing mopping-up activities in the village of Gornji Prhovo and the civilian Brane Davic killed in the hamlet of Skrbici. It talks about crushing the resistance of extremists and fundamentalists. How long did any resistance last, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the resistance lasted two days. After two days, when negotiations were asked that Omer should make it possible for secure -- to take out the body of Duce and Omer should surrender and all the civilians would be saved and Serbs would not be Serbs if they did not keep their words, and they have been doing this for several hundreds of years. After Omer surrendered from all the weapons, all these villages were fired upon from Brescica so that all the casualties mentioned here were casualties of helpless people who were killed by mortars and by other weapons. Ratko Bulac was commander of the unit and Marko Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Thank you, Mr. Filipovic. We'll have a break of 15 to 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to -- oh, sorry, I see Mr. Ackerman on his feet. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm able to report that the name of the commentator is Hajdar Zimmerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry -- well, I was going to talk about the video anyhow. But do I understand that Mr. Ackerman is confirming from his own information that Zimmerman is the name of the reporter, despite the lack of belief that this was a Bosnian name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't I just say that the name of the reporter is Hajdar Zimmerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I just said that. Didn't I just say that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I was just checking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zimmerman is also amongst the Maltese names. So it's not just --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's a very common Bosnian name, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And -- this was said in the absence of Mr. Filipovic, so I think we ought to confirm that we're grateful to Mr. Filipovic for making the inquiry overnight. But Your Honour, on the subject of the video, I understand it was given to the -- to the Court, because did I have it made an exhibit yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking the Court to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I know Your Honours haven't. Oh, the Registry, do you have the video now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then I wonder if it could be handed to the technicians now in advance, and if it could be -- if we can try to get it to the part where -- at the end of the bullfighting or whatever, the fiesta scenes. And on my guess it's around 22 minutes or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, have you still got the report that we were looking at, because I just want to deal with some other aspects of it. It's the structure that -- no, I'm sorry. Paragraph 3, "Protection and confiscation of weapons." If we could just deal with that. "The public security station in the course of its activities and in keeping with a decision of the Crisis Staff collected 270 legally owned hunting rifles and 200 legally owned pistols. And then the following, illegally owned weapons, 100 automatic rifles, 9 semi-automatic, and 9 submachine-guns, 45 hunting rifles, one 60-millimetre mortar, 40 pistols," and so on and so forth. "And according to our assessments, public security station employees confiscated over 60 per cent of illegally owned weapons. The fact that no weapons were found in the possession of members of military units presented a special problem in this work." And then it talks about "A certain number of automatic weapons, hand grenades, and a few Zolja hand-held rocket launchers were taken away by the worst extremists and fundamentalists who fled in the direction of Bihac, estimation number of 200." And I think we're going to come to another estimate of weapons in a moment. Can we look then at the structure and the composition of the so-called Muslim Territorial Defence, paragraph 4: "The structure of units of the so-called Muslim Territorial Defence was explained in the introduction. All the information we obtained during our operations was quite accurate." Can I just pause there for a moment, Mr. Filipovic. Were you aware that, as it were, members of the Serbian security forces were obtaining information about the Muslim Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is called spying, espionage. They were spying on us. And in various ways, they obtained information about us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you appreciate that at the time, that they were getting accurate information about your numbers and your weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We assumed that they knew this. In my statements I always use the figure of 500 to 700 men, and they knew that. There were 500 to 700 men that were loyal to their city, to their people, and to their state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then it lists there the various people who were involved. There was a Colonel Efendic who was the commander of the Territorial Defence staff; your brother.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to correct you. It says here "Colonel Hasan Efendic, commander of the staff." He was commander of the Bosnian staff in Sarajevo in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he appointed Omer Filipovic; therefore, he was legally elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minister or whatever position he had. Those are the people who do the appointments, not people who organised a revolution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then it goes on to name various people. You've told us about Mr. Avdic, and then Mr. Egrlic, Mr. Kapetanovic, and then the Crisis Staff that you have also told us about. So clearly they did have good information. It then goes on to list --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to -- I apologise. Kapetanovic Emir, he was in the building where the Bosnian Municipality of Kljuc was housed. He had his surgery. And by chance when a part of Velagici was attacked, he stayed behind there. So -- and he's a physician, a gynaecologist, a specialist. And he had his own surgery there. And on the tape that I have provided, you will find that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that he was not in the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're about to watch the tape in a moment. I just want to finish the document, Mr. Filipovic. Then they list what they say are the various companies and the heads of these companies, and then they say, "Based on information obtained through operational work, the so-called Muslim Territorial Defence numbered between 1.300 and 1.500 people, most of them did not have uniforms nor did they receive the appropriate insignia." The figure, 13 to 15 hundred people, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. It says here "through operational work." They don't want to say that at Manjaca and in Stara Gradiska by beating they obtained confessions from people saying that they were members. If you beat somebody unconscious, if you use an axle or a 2-inch telephone cable, a man would admit that he's a Martian, not to mention a member of the Territorial Defence, just to stay alive. Therefore, these operational information was information obtained by investigators at Manjaca through beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "According to our checks, they had available 800 guns of all types (including legally owned weapons)." And I think you've already told us that you described the weaponry. Now, there's some more to this report, although I think at this stage -- yes, can we just look, please, at paragraph 8, which is headed "Prevention and detection of persons responsible for criminal acts," where it states that "A large number of criminal acts were committed in the course of combat activities. They were mostly serious thefts and arson. A large number of houses located in Pudin Han, Velagici, Donji Biljani, Sanica, Prhovo, and Plamenice were destroyed and set alight." It is suggested that effectively these were isolated criminal acts. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that they were isolated acts. These were acts by obedients who plundered, and making a certain gain they distributed the looty to the leaders, because they went to war to rob us, to loot us, because they thought until the end of their lives they could keep what they stole from the Muslims and Croats. There isn't a house from which they didn't steal something ranging from furniture, cars, not to mention human lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You can put that report aside. And then can we just deal with a few of these other documents that deal with these incidents. Could you be handed P915, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that's back to volume 1. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a report, a news broadcast from Banja Luka Radio/Television, which deals with the -- that report. And as you rightly point out, here we have the correct village. "At around noon Muslim extremists from the village of Krasulje in the Kljuc municipality ambushed and killed deputy commander of the Kljuc public security station, Dusan Stojakovic. After that villagers joined by Muslim fundamentalists from the neighbouring village of Velagici skirmished with the police." Can you then, please, be shown document 916, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, I should say, is objected to, and it is specifically objected to. It's a record of the Kljuc Municipality Crisis Staff meeting held at 8.00 on the 28th of May. Again, the order was that there was to be a surrender of weapons and if they do not, thorough measures will be undertaken to disarm them, which may have disastrous consequences for their personal safety, for that of their property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about earlier disarmament calls, and you said you hadn't heard anything. Do you recall, however - or were you already arrested in the early hours of the 28th of May - a call for the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 8.00, and on the 28th of May at 10.30 I was arrested. And one of my neighbours around 9.30 told me, using my nickname, Muhis, "They're asking that you surrender on Radio Kljuc and they went to your house." So I arrived home around 10.00, I think it was, and my legal weapon for which I had a licence, having first searched the house as in a crime film, they took away my weapon without any receipt or anything. So it's nothing more than looting. So they arrested me at 10.30 some 200 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We then see that there's a call in relation to the commander of the police station, that there should be -- and the Muslims from Velagici and Pudin Han ordered to surrender the perpetrators of the crime against the convoy. And then over the page, "The commander of the so-called Territorial Defence and Green Berets, Omer Filipovic, is hereby called upon to surrender to the legal --" sorry, it's not over the page. It's paragraph 5 for you -- "is hereby called upon to surrender the legal -- to the legal military forces of the Serbian Republic. "6, all members of the armed forces from Kljuc and the White Eagles who have returned from Kupres, are hereby ordered to place themselves under the command of the 30th Division." And then: "Citizens requested to remain calm." Did you hear on the radio a call -- you say you were told by your neighbour there was a call for you to surrender, but for your brother to surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also for him. This call was addressed to him too. And here it mentions the White Eagles, a paramilitary Chetnik formation. So under the alleged legal Serbian forces, there were the paramilitary Chetnik forces, called the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just checking something. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I need to ask you on those documents. There are a series of Defence -- of documents issued to the command of the defence of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just want to check, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you look now, please, at Exhibit 922. Again, in relation to your brother. This was apparently a radio statement of the command of the Kljuc defence, an announcement that citizens -- it's quite difficult to read because there's a lot crossed out. But "Citizens of Muslim nationality are being informed about the latest agreement between Omer Filipovic, the commander of the so-called Muslim Territorial Defence and the command of the Kljuc defence." And then it makes -- it gives various demands for surrender of various Muslims. And then it states at the bottom: "In case of non-observance of the said provisions of this agreement, it will be considered as if they are in an armed conflict and measures will be taken towards them as towards all enemies." And then apparently something. "Dear listeners, fierce armed conflicts between legal Serbian defence forces and the Muslim paramilitaries in the areas of Kljuc, Sehici, Pudin Han, Velagici, Ramici, and Krasulje, the resistance of the illegal Muslim forces in this area has been broken. That was the main reason for the earlier achieved agreement." And then in connection with that, Exhibit, please, P923. Again, this is an order from the same date, stating "Since Mr. Omer Filipovic on behalf of the Muslims and all the people who possess weapons has asked for a postponement of the deadline until 10.00 hours on the 29th of May and in token of understanding for this proposal, the Kljuc defence command has accepted his proposal under the condition seven captured soldiers," et cetera, et cetera. Obviously by this stage, at 4.00, you were already in custody, Mr. Filipovic. But whilst you were in custody, did you become aware of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. This was the 29th. And on the 29th I was already in Stara Gradiska in another state. Stara Gradiska is not Bosnia-Herzegovina but the Republic of Croatia. So on the 28th I was transferred -- I was captured and transferred. I can say what I know about this. They did not respect the agreement reached with Omer Filipovic. The order was and the agreement was for Omer to surrender and for all civilians to be released home. However, before this break I said that after Omer entered the police car, from all sides a cannonade of shells fell on Pudin Han and Velagici, so that they did not abide by the agreement and Omer was captured and taken to Stara Gradiska as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you, Mr. Filipovic. I think now the thing to do would be to ask that the video that was made could be played. Mr. Filipovic, if there's any point at which you wish to make a comment about what we see, if you just say "stop" into the microphone, the technicians will stop it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like know whether they are expected to translate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We establish that there was a link between the official leaderships of the SDA and the Muslim Bosniak party and that the leaders of those parties were directly involved in the procurement of weapons, the formation of units, and that this whole process was organised through the parties."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we pause for a moment. Can we pause.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The municipality of Kljuc had 37.000 inhabitants."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. The gentleman we just saw, we've all been told who it is. But could you identify him for us, please, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my former friend Vinko Kondic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask, this video recording goes back to 1992, I would imagine. No? Which -- which particular period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, can you assist? This video recording, I know it was sent to you, but can you say what period of 1992 this was from what's on the film?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recording was made in my assessment at the beginning of June 1992. It was a recording made by Banja Luka Television. And I received a copy in 1993 in England from a friend in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "in your opinion it was made in June 1992," what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base it on the fact that it is immediately after the conflict which occurred on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of May. So immediately after that one can see destruction. And there's also some data. For instance, what was filmed in Kljuc, you can establish the date. My theory may not be correct, because you can see on the recording that he's in Kljuc. One can find out when the mosque was destroyed. So then recording was done after that, because it can be established when the mosque was destroyed, or it may be the filming was in two parts, in Kljuc and Velagici. I assume that this in Velagici was in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we could carry on playing the video. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] There were 49 per cent are Serbs, 44.5 per cent Muslims, 0.9 per cent Croats, and 5.6 per cent Yugoslavs and others. These wartime events have left their imprint on this environment and will effect overall developments in Kljuc municipality in many ways. The Crisis Staff is taking over power. Many decisions have been taken, including the introduction of a curfew, the stopping of work of all companies and most other establishments, which means switching to wartime conditions. During the last few days the Crisis Staff has issued an order that citizens may move from 7 to 20 hours that, shops will also be working --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. You can see here that the mosque is intact. So if we can find the date of the demolition of the mosque, we can establish that the film was made before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have a date, and I'll -- there's a document that gives it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, could we carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Spirits can be served up to 6.00 p.m. What is most important, decisions have been taken on the working hours of enterprises and especially of Sip Kljuc in which the annual maintenance we begin a month ahead of time. As of 20th of June, a regular line Vrbljani-Banja Luka through Sitnica has been introduced. The bus will be leaving at 5.30 and from Kljuc at 7.00 and from Banja Luka at 3.00. Also, other bus lines will be introduced at the level of Kljuc and other neighbouring municipalities. The wartime activities in Kljuc have left tragic consequences, as is the case in many other areas, because they have refused to surrender their weapons and declare that they want to fight. The representatives of villages inhabited exclusively by Muslims have got what they wanted. Negotiations were conducted with the most extreme forces, and their response was that they do not want the civilian population to suffer but that they would not suffer under any circumstances and that they would fight to the death rather than surrender and disarm. So this was an extremist wing which gives a real picture of Muslim fundamentalism. In the area of Kljuc municipality, by operational work we have established that there's a link between the official leadership of the Party of Democratic Action and the Muslim Bosniak organisation and party and that the leaders of these parties were directly involved in the procurement of weapons, the formation of units, and that this whole process was organised via the parties. Tell us, what happened when it became clear that they do not wish to negotiate or to hand over the weapons, that they want war. What did the Serbian side do? What did the police do? We responded by setting ultimatums for deadlines for the surrender of weapons and we said that after that we would destroy the enemy forces and that we would protect the civilian population in the area because there were cases when they threatened the entire civilian population. They opened fire at their own civilians, and they would not allow the civilians to flee to certain localities. When talking about these villages -- The fiercest fighting was in Pudin Han, Velagici, Gornji Ramici, and to a certain extent in Donja Sanica, boarding on Sanski Most the villages of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, which are known from before as the greatest strongholds of Muslim fundamentalists.
